aspects.says: Predicate.and and or evaluate the receiver first and the argument only when the receiver hasn't decided the result, so a guard placed first protects the checks after it.
basis: section:andThen Runs the Receiver First and compose the Argument First; and/or Stop Early

aspects.says: f.andThen(g) applies f and then g to its result; f.compose(g) applies g first.
basis: section:andThen Runs the Receiver First and compose the Argument First; and/or Stop Early

aspects.says: @FunctionalInterface doesn't make an interface a lambda target; it makes javac reject a second abstract method at the interface, where without it the error appears only where a lambda targets it.
basis: section:One Abstract Method Makes an Interface Functional; @FunctionalInterface Only Checks It

aspects.says: Function<Integer, Integer> allocates two Integers per call wherever the JIT can't inline the lambda, as at a call site that sees several lambdas; the primitive specialisations never box.
basis: section:Function<Integer, Integer> Boxes Each Value Unless the JIT Removes It; IntUnaryOperator Never Boxes

aspects.says: A lambda passed to Comparator.comparing gets no target type when reversed() is called on the result, so its parameter is Object and the call doesn't compile.
basis: section:reversed() Reverses the Whole Comparator Chain Built Before It
aspects.reason: a compile-time rule: no wrong solution compiles against a fixed test, and the type inference behind it is unit 4.1.1's subject

aspects.says: An interface is functional when exactly one abstract method is left after default and static methods and abstract redeclarations of Object's public methods, so Comparator, which also declares equals, is functional.
basis: section:One Abstract Method Makes an Interface Functional; @FunctionalInterface Only Checks It

aspects.says: reversed() on a chained comparator reverses every key in the chain; one key is reversed by giving its thenComparing a reverse-order comparator.
basis: section:reversed() Reverses the Whole Comparator Chain Built Before It

aspects.says: Two functional interfaces of the same shape are unrelated types: a value of one can't be passed as the other, and needs an adapter such as a method reference.
basis: section:Use java.util.function Until a Name, a Checked Exception or a Third Parameter Asks for Your Own

aspects.says: Prefer java.util.function, and declare your own interface for a domain name, a checked exception or three or more parameters.
basis: section:Use java.util.function Until a Name, a Checked Exception or a Third Parameter Asks for Your Own
aspects.reason: a design judgement with more than one defensible answer; no deterministic test can grade it, and the checkout practice already hands the reader a domain interface to work with

aspects.says: A method that takes Function<T, R> rejects a Function<Object, String> for a List<Integer>; Function<? super T, ? extends R> accepts it.
basis: section:Accept Function<? super T, ? extends R>, or Callers' Functions Don't Fit
